title: Language Models for Text Classification: From Bag-of-Words to Jev
author: Sebastian Raschka
updated_note: the first archived copy (29 September 11:07 UTC, 17 minutes after publication) has no Section 5.3 and no updates; by 20:18 UTC the author had added Section 5.3 (answering a reader's question) and Updates 1 and 2; by 2 October, the 1961 naive Bayes reference, a missing symbol in the RLCR reward and the note that calibration worsened one of nine datasets, each prompted by a reader comment
takeaway: A free long explainer (about 36 minutes, 39 figures, linked code) that follows text classification on IMDb reviews from bag-of-words logistic regression (89.9%) through LSTMs, CNNs and fine-tuned transformers to TypeSafe's Jev decision model, which scored 96.47% on the 25,000 test reviews with no IMDb training for $0.65 in one run by the author; it sketches a Jev-like API on any transformer and relates Jev's unpublished training method to RLCR, a published reward for calibrated confidence.
verdict: A clear, correct history and an honest hands-on test of Jev; read the IMDb numbers as single runs on three different test sets of a benchmark Jev may have seen. The Jev-like design and the guess of a small ModernBERT-like model are not how Jev works: earlier measurements show it reads its options together and has frontier-scale knowledge, and the benchmark the article cites found Jev badly calibrated on one of three datasets.

headline.k: Jev's Choice API on the 25,000 test reviews, no IMDb training, 22 minutes and $0.6492; Noul gave 96.20%
headline.d: one run each by the author; IMDb may be in Jev's training data

headline.k: the logistic regression baseline he still starts with; an LSTM from scratch got 85.66%, pretrained ULMFiT 95.4%
headline.d: from his notebooks; three different test sets across the ladder

headline.k: RLCR against plain RLVR on HotpotQA (Qwen2.5-7B) at 62.1% against 63.0% accuracy
headline.at: reduces expected calibration error (ECE) from 0.37 to 0.03

more_note: Section 1 is the pre-transformer history, Section 2 the three transformer families as classifiers, Sections 3 to 6 Jev: its API, an IMDb run, a Jev-like design, calibration and RLCR, and who it is for.

responses.n: Twelve days before the article, from about 10,000 API calls: 84.6% on MMLU-Pro (frontier-scale knowledge); an irrelevant fifth option lowered the log-odds between two others from +0.38 to +0.11 in all ten blocks, so Jev reads its options together. The article does not cite it.

responses.t: BTZSC pilot v1: Jev against GLiNER2.5
responses.n: Preregistered, 100 examples per dataset: Jev far more accurate on AG News (0.910 against 0.700) and Banking77 (0.870 against 0.610), tied on emotion with much worse probabilities (ECE 0.351 against 0.117). The article quotes it only as Jev being stronger.
The author agreed it is, in expectation, cited Guo et al. on overfitting the log-likelihood, and wrote the answer into the post as Section 5.3 the same day.

responses.t: Temperature scaling is brittle under shift
responses.n: A calibration researcher: one fitted temperature breaks under covariate shift, where an agent's branches lead, and a decision model must be sharp as well as calibrated; he cited his own SDM activations (arXiv 2509.12760). No reply by 27 November.

responses.t: One pass for all options, or a 255-slot head?
responses.n: Section 4's design runs one forward pass per option; one reader proposed one input with a classification token per option, another a fixed 255-way head with unused slots masked. No reply by 27 November.

responses.t: TF-IDF still beats Jev in many enterprise jobs. Here is where Jev wins.
responses.n: Jev against TF-IDF and a fine-tuned mmBERT on human labels: behind on complaint issues (46.6% against 61.2%); 1.00 on 581 of 1,000 complaints but right on 90.2% of those, so no threshold reached 95%; one ordinary sentence moved 55% of its decisions. Jev won on checking AI answers and on unseen languages.

since.n: Update 1's API reached public beta on GPT-6 Luna at $0.10 per million input tokens, output free; Cloudflare, Amazon and Microsoft shipped the same shape.
Better multilingual support (the weak spot the article reports), images in requests, a Box question type, 262k-token context.

resources.n: The launch post: RLCD named but not defined, parallel sampling, $0.042 per million input tokens, the workflow evals scored against GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 as reference, and the FAQ's "Jev is neither small nor an LLM".

resources.t: TypeSafe docs: Confidence and Model jaggedness
resources.n: How the confidence field is computed from the probabilities, and the known failure modes, including Choice answers that lean toward the first option.

resources.t: Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty
resources.by: Damani, Puri, Slocum, Shenfeld, Choshen, Kim, Andreas (MIT), 2025 (maker)
resources.n: RLCR: the reward c minus (q minus c) squared, its proof that honest confidence maximises it, and Table 1, whose numbers Section 5.2 quotes.

resources.t: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
resources.n: Why deep classifiers become overconfident while accuracy improves, and temperature scaling as the fix: the basis of Sections 5.1 and 5.3.

resources.t: Universal Language Model Fine-tuning for Text Classification (ULMFiT)
resources.n: Pretrain a language model, fine-tune it, then the classifier: 4.6% error on IMDb, the transfer-learning step between the LSTM and BERT.
The code behind the GPT-2 and ModernBERT numbers of Section 2 (91.88% and 95.07%), on a 35,000/5,000/10,000 reshuffle of all 50,000 reviews, not the official test set.

kb.n: Owns Jev as a product (System One models, RLCD as TypeSafe describes it, prices and vendor speed claims) and the decision-model tier that followed it.
Decision models as the classifier-shaped judge, and fitting the threshold on a labelled slice instead of leaving it at 0.5.
Logistic regression and naive Bayes, including why naive Bayes probabilities come out overconfident.
RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs and static word vectors (real GloVe), the article's Sections 1.2.1 and 1.2.2.

kb.t: Families and objectives: decoder-only, encoders, encoder-decoder, multi-token prediction, diffusion LMs
kb.n: Encoders, decoders and T5-style encoder-decoders, their masks and objectives, ModernBERT, and why encoders win classification at equal size (Ettin).

kb.t: Probability for ML: random variables, distributions to losses, MLE, MAP, Bayes
kb.n: Proper scoring rules, reliability diagrams and temperature scaling measured on real models.
Log-loss, Brier and ECE, with a real naive Bayes model recalibrated.

kb.t: RL for LLMs: RLHF, GRPO, RLVR
kb.n: RLVR's binary reward, which RLCR extends with a calibration term.

kb.t: Rerankers and late interaction: cross-encoders, ColBERT, LLM rerankers
kb.n: Cross-encoders score one query and document pair per pass, the same shape as Section 4's per-candidate scorer; listwise LLM rerankers read all candidates at once.

kb.t: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
kb.n: The paper page behind Section 2.1's classification token.
"Decision models became a product category in two weeks": the Decisions API, Clef, Strands Decider and serving-engine support.

topics.n: encoders, decoders and encoder-decoders as classifiers
